title: Retirement and Death of a Partner
summary: On the retirement or death of a partner the firm is reconstituted, and the amount due to the outgoing partner or his executors must be worked out and settled. This chapter covers new and gaining ratios, adjustment of goodwill, revaluation, reserves, share of profit up to the date of death, and settlement through cash, loan or instalments.

notes.heading: Retirement and death: adjustments required
notes.html:
A partner may retire by giving notice (in a partnership at will), with the consent of all partners, or as provided in the deed. On death, the firm normally continues with the remaining partners, and the deceased partner's dues are paid to his legal representatives (executors).

Adjustments required:

  1. New profit-sharing ratio and gaining ratio of continuing partners
  2. Treatment of goodwill
  3. Revaluation of assets and liabilities
  4. Distribution of accumulated profits, reserves and losses
  5. Share of profit/loss up to the date of retirement or death (if during the year)
  6. Settlement of the amount due to the retiring partner or executors
  7. Adjustment of continuing partners' capitals (if required)

notes.heading: New ratio and gaining ratio
notes.html:
Gaining ratio = New ratio − Old ratio of each continuing partner. It is used to debit continuing partners for the retiring partner's share of goodwill.

CaseIllustration
Nothing is statedContinuing partners keep their old ratio; gaining ratio = their old ratio. A, B, C 5:3:2; C retires: new ratio 5:3; gaining ratio 5:3.
New ratio of continuing partners is givenA, B, C 5:3:2; B retires; A and C agree to share 3:2. A gains 3/5 − 5/10 = 1/10; C gains 2/5 − 2/10 = 2/10. Gaining ratio 1:2.
Retiring partner's share is taken in a stated proportionP, Q, R 4:3:2; Q retires; P and R take his share equally. P = 4/9 + 3/18 = 11/18; R = 2/9 + 3/18 = 7/18. Gaining ratio 1:1.

Occasionally the agreed new ratio makes a continuing partner's new share smaller than his old share. That partner then sacrifices along with the retiring partner and is credited (not debited) in the goodwill entry.

notes.heading: Treatment of goodwill
notes.html:
The retiring or deceased partner is compensated for his share of goodwill by the gaining partners in the gaining ratio, without raising goodwill in the books (AS-26).

SituationJournal entry
Existing goodwill in the booksAll Partners' Capital A/cs Dr (old ratio) To Goodwill A/c
Retiring partner's share of goodwillContinuing (gaining) Partners' Capital A/cs Dr (gaining ratio) To Retiring Partner's Capital A/c

Example: A, B, C share 5:3:2; B retires; A and C share 3:2 in future (gaining ratio 1:2). Goodwill ₹1,00,000. B's share = ₹30,000. Entry: A's Capital A/c Dr ₹10,000; C's Capital A/c Dr ₹20,000 To B's Capital A/c ₹30,000.

notes.heading: Revaluation and reserves
notes.html:
• A Revaluation Account is prepared; profit or loss is shared by all partners, including the retiring/deceased partner, in the old ratio.
  • Reserves and accumulated profits are credited, and accumulated losses debited, to all partners in the old ratio.
  • If the continuing partners want assets, liabilities and reserves at old values, only the retiring partner's share is adjusted: Gaining Partners' Capital A/cs Dr To Retiring Partner's Capital A/c (for his share of reserves and revaluation profit), and the reverse for losses.

notes.heading: Comprehensive worked illustration: retirement
notes.html:
X, Y and Z share profits 2:2:1. Z retires on 31 March 2025. Balance Sheet: Creditors ₹40,000; General Reserve ₹50,000; Capitals X ₹1,00,000, Y ₹1,00,000, Z ₹80,000 (total ₹3,70,000). Assets: Bank ₹30,000; Debtors ₹60,000; Stock ₹80,000; Machinery ₹1,20,000; Building ₹80,000 (total ₹3,70,000). Building is appreciated by ₹20,000; stock is reduced by ₹5,000; goodwill is valued at ₹75,000. Z is paid ₹28,000 immediately and the balance is transferred to his loan account.

Revaluation profit = 20,000 − 5,000 = ₹15,000 (X 6,000; Y 6,000; Z 3,000). Z's share of goodwill = 75,000 x 1/5 = ₹15,000, borne by X and Y in gaining ratio 1:1 (₹7,500 each).

notes.heading: Settlement of the amount due
notes.html:
The amount due may be paid in a lump sum, transferred to the retiring partner's loan account, or paid in instalments with interest. Under Section 37 of the Partnership Act, until the amount is paid, the outgoing partner (or his estate) is entitled, at his option, to interest @ 6% p.a. on the amount due or to the share of profits earned by use of that amount.

Worked illustration: loan repaid in instalments

Z's loan of ₹80,000 is repaid in 4 equal annual instalments of principal plus interest @ 10% p.a. on the outstanding balance.

notes.heading: Death of a partner: share of profit up to the date of death
notes.html:
If death occurs during the year, the deceased partner's share of profit from the start of the year to the date of death is credited to his capital account, usually without closing the books:

  • Time basis: Share = Last year's (or average) profit x Months up to death/12 x Deceased's share.
  • Turnover (sales) basis: Profit up to death = Sales up to death x Last year's profit/Last year's sales; Share = that profit x Deceased's share.

Entry: Profit and Loss Suspense A/c Dr To Deceased Partner's Capital A/c. (Alternatively, if the gaining partners are to bear it: Continuing Partners' Capital A/cs Dr in gaining ratio To Deceased Partner's Capital A/c.) The P&L Suspense balance is closed to the Profit and Loss Account at the end of the year.

Worked illustration

P, Q, R share 3:2:1. R dies on 30 June 2025; accounting year begins 1 April. Last year's profit ₹1,20,000 on sales of ₹8,00,000. Sales from 1 April to 30 June 2025 were ₹3,00,000.

  • Time basis: 1,20,000 x 3/12 x 1/6 = ₹5,000
  • Turnover basis: profit rate = 1,20,000/8,00,000 = 15%; profit up to death = 3,00,000 x 15% = ₹45,000; R's share = 45,000 x 1/6 = ₹7,500

The balance of the deceased partner's capital account is transferred to Deceased Partner's Executors Account: Deceased Partner's Capital A/c Dr To His Executors A/c.

notes.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
notes.html:
• Debiting the retiring partner's goodwill share to continuing partners in the old ratio when the gaining ratio is different.
  • Excluding the retiring partner from revaluation profit or reserves; he shares them in the old ratio.
  • Charging interest on the loan for the first year on the reduced balance instead of the opening balance.
  • Calculating the deceased partner's profit share for the whole year instead of up to the date of death.
  • Forgetting interest on capital and drawings up to the date of death when given.

keyTerms.definition: Withdrawal of a partner from the firm while the remaining partners continue the business.
Ratio in which continuing partners acquire the share of the retiring or deceased partner; New ratio − Old ratio.
Account to which the unpaid amount due to a retiring partner is transferred; treated as an outside liability.
Legal representatives of a deceased partner who receive the amount due to him.
Temporary account debited with the deceased partner's share of profit up to the date of death when books are not closed.
Method of estimating profit up to death in proportion to the time elapsed in the year.
Method of estimating profit up to death on the basis of sales made up to that date at last year's rate of profit.
Provision entitling an outgoing partner to interest @ 6% p.a. or a share of profits earned on his unpaid dues, at his option.
Insurance policy on the lives of all partners jointly; the sum assured is payable to the firm on the death of any partner.
Account recording changes in asset and liability values on reconstitution; shared by all old partners in old ratio.

formulas.html: Continuing partners' old ratio becomes their new ratio

formulas.name: Retiring partner's share of goodwill
formulas.html: Firm's goodwill x Retiring partner's share

formulas.name: Profit up to death (time basis)
formulas.html: Base profit x Months up to death/12 x Deceased partner's share

formulas.name: Profit up to death (turnover basis)
formulas.html: Sales up to death x (Last year's profit / Last year's sales) x Deceased partner's share

formulas.name: Amount due to retiring partner
formulas.html: Capital + Share of reserves + Share of revaluation profit + Share of goodwill + Interest on capital + Salary/profit to date − Drawings − Interest on drawings − Share of losses

formulas.name: Instalment with interest
formulas.html: Equal principal instalment + Interest on opening balance of the loan

mcqs.explanation: A continuing partner gains when his new share is more than his old share.

mcqs.q: A, B and C share 5:3:2. B retires and A and C decide to share future profits 3:2. The gaining ratio is:
On retirement, the retiring partner's share of goodwill is debited to:
options: Retiring partner's capital account
Continuing partners' capital accounts in gaining ratio
Goodwill account
Revaluation account
mcqs.explanation: The continuing partners who gain his share compensate him in the gaining ratio.

mcqs.q: R, a partner with 1/6 share, died on 30 June. The accounting year starts on 1 April. Last year's profit was ₹1,20,000. His share of profit till death on time basis is:

Assertion (A): The amount remaining unpaid to a retiring partner is transferred to his loan account.
Reason (R): Under Section 37, an outgoing partner may claim, at his option, interest @ 6% p.a. or a share of profits earned with his unpaid amount.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Both statements are correct, but the transfer to a loan account is a recording practice for an outside liability; it is not explained by the right to interest.

mcqs.q: Case: Last year's sales were ₹8,00,000 and profit ₹1,20,000. A partner with 1/6 share died after sales of ₹3,00,000 had been made in the current year. His share of profit up to death on turnover basis is:
mcqs.explanation: Profit rate 15%; profit up to death = ₹45,000; share = 45,000 x 1/6 = ₹7,500.

mcqs.q: When a deceased partner's share of profit up to the date of death is credited to him without closing the books, the account debited is:
options: Profit and Loss Suspense A/c
Revaluation A/c
Realisation A/c
Executors A/c
mcqs.explanation: P&L Suspense A/c is debited temporarily and closed to the P&L Account at year-end.

mcqs.q: If nothing is said about how the continuing partners will share the retiring partner's share, the gaining ratio is:
options: Equal ratio
Sacrificing ratio
Old ratio of the continuing partners
Ratio of their capitals
mcqs.explanation: They are presumed to continue in their old ratio, so they gain in that same ratio.

mcqs.q: Z, a retiring partner, has a capital of ₹80,000, share of reserve ₹10,000, share of revaluation profit ₹3,000 and share of goodwill ₹15,000. The amount due to Z is:

Assertion (A): Profit on revaluation at the time of retirement is shared by all partners, including the retiring partner, in the old ratio.
Reason (R): The change in values relates to the period during which the retiring partner was a partner.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: The retiring partner is entitled to his share of increase in values that arose while he was a partner; R explains A.

mcqs.q: A retiring partner's loan of ₹80,000 is repayable in 4 equal annual instalments with interest @ 10% p.a. on the balance. The total payment at the end of the first year is:

Assertion (A): The retiring partner's share of goodwill is credited to all partners' capital accounts in the new ratio.
Reason (R): Goodwill compensates the retiring partner for the share of future profits he gives up.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: A is false: his share is credited to the retiring partner and debited to gaining partners. R correctly states the purpose.

questions.q: What is meant by gaining ratio?
questions.answerHtml: Gaining ratio is the ratio in which the continuing partners acquire the share of profit of the retiring or deceased partner. Gaining ratio = New ratio − Old ratio.

questions.q: Name the two methods of calculating a deceased partner's share of profit from the beginning of the year to the date of death.
questions.answerHtml:
• Time basis (on the basis of last year's or average profit)
  • Turnover or sales basis

questions.q: P, Q and R share profits 4:3:2. Q retires and his share is taken by P and R equally. Goodwill of the firm is valued at ₹1,80,000. Calculate the new ratio and gaining ratio and pass the entry for goodwill.
questions.answerHtml:
Q's share 3/9 is taken equally: 3/18 each.

  • P = 4/9 + 3/18 = 11/18; R = 2/9 + 3/18 = 7/18. New ratio 11:7.
  • Gaining ratio = 3/18 : 3/18 = 1:1.

Q's share of goodwill = 1,80,000 x 3/9 = ₹60,000.

Last year's sales were ₹20,00,000 and profit ₹3,00,000; sales from 1 April to 31 August 2025 were ₹6,00,000. Calculate D's share of profit on (a) time basis (average profit) and (b) turnover basis, and pass the entry for (a).
questions.answerHtml:
1. Time basis: 1,80,000 x 5/12 x 1/4 = ₹18,750
  2. Turnover basis: Profit rate = 3,00,000/20,00,000 = 15%. Profit up to death = 6,00,000 x 15% = ₹90,000. D's share = 90,000 x 1/4 = ₹22,500

Entry (a): Profit and Loss Suspense A/c Dr ₹18,750 To D's Capital A/c ₹18,750.

questions.q: Explain the treatment of reserves and revaluation profit on retirement when the continuing partners do not want to change the book values. Illustrate: A, B, C share 2:2:1; C retires; reserve ₹40,000 and revaluation profit ₹10,000 are not to be shown; A and B continue equally.
questions.answerHtml:
When book values are not to be changed, only the retiring partner's share is credited to him and debited to the gaining partners in gaining ratio.

  • C's share = (40,000 + 10,000) x 1/5 = ₹10,000.
  • Gain: A 1/2 − 2/5 = 1/10; B 1/2 − 2/5 = 1/10; gaining ratio 1:1.
